script.opening: (Anxious, talking quickly.) "I've been on the mini-pill — desogestrel — for about eight months, and my periods have basically stopped. I read that can happen, but now I'm paranoid — what if I'm actually pregnant and don't know? Is no periods normal on this, or should I be worried?"

facts.text: First four months: light, irregular spotting. Last four months: nothing at all. No bleeding after sex.

"Mostly in the morning. I think I've been good, but I can't swear I've never been late." Uses a phone alarm. Has she missed any? "Not that I remember, but I couldn't be certain." Last possibly late pill: a weekend about two weeks ago — maybe 4–5 hours late, within 12 hours.
No vomiting or diarrhoea. "No, nothing like that" — no antibiotics, St John's wort, epilepsy medicines or other new medicines. No allergies.
"Not really. I'm just anxious." No nausea, breast tenderness or tiredness. Last unprotected sex: regular sex with her partner on the pill only; last sex 4 days ago. No pregnancy test done.

Partner of 6 months, Kieran. No STI test since they got together; previous partner a year ago. No discharge, pain or pelvic pain. Cervical screening: "I'd need to check on the smear" — had one at 25, normal.
Well. Non-smoker. Retail supervisor. Chose the mini-pill because the combined pill gave her migraines with flashing lights.
"It's not the right time. I just want to know the pill's actually working." Wants children in a few years; worries a bit whether no periods will affect fertility.

Anxious, wants reassurance — but if the doctor simply says "that's normal" without asking about pills or suggesting a test, stay worried: "But how do you know I'm not pregnant?" Happy to do a test: "I can get one from the chemist on the way home." Calms when the plan is clear.

ice.ideas: "It might be the pill — or I might be pregnant."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of an unplanned pregnancy; quietly wondering whether having no periods could affect her fertility later.
ice.expectations: "To know whether no periods is normal — and that the pill is working."

cues: "I can't swear I've never been late." — invites checking pill-taking.
"I'm paranoid." — the anxiety to take seriously.
"Will it affect having kids later?" — only if her worries are explored.

checkpoints.text: Reassures ACCURATELY that amenorrhoea/erratic bleeding is a common, acceptable and expected effect of the desogestrel POP (and not a sign of failure) — but only AFTER excluding pregnancy

Applies "reassure, but TEST FIRST": screens missed/late pills (12-hour window), vomiting/diarrhoea, interacting medications and pregnancy symptoms, and arranges a PREGNANCY TEST where there is any doubt (home urine test reported back, as it cannot be done on video; repeated if within 3 weeks of unprotected sex)
Reviews correct POP use and reinforces the missed-pill rules (late >12h → take pill, 48h condoms; vomiting/diarrhoea within the CoSRH time limit as missed; emergency contraception if indicated)
Performs a wider sexual-health review — STI risk/testing, cervical screening status, and whether the method still suits her (consider LARC if bleeding bothersome)
Addresses the REAL worry: once pregnancy is excluded and use is correct, gives confident, explained reassurance and states what would warrant rechecking
Takes the pregnancy anxiety seriously rather than waving it away, and explores any unspoken concerns (method suitability, future fertility)
Makes the reassurance land by basing it on the test and her usage, checking understanding
Safety-nets and follows up: when to retest, missed-pill/EC advice, screening/STI follow-up, and method review — informed reassurance, not a brush-off

worked.txt: "Good question, and I’m glad you asked rather than worrying alone. The short version is: yes, no periods is usually normal on this pill — but the right thing for me to do is make sure you’re not pregnant first, and then reassure you properly."

"Have you missed or been late with any pills — more than 12 hours — or had vomiting or a tummy bug, or started any new medicines? … I’d like you to do a pregnancy test too, just so we both know for certain rather than guessing — you can do a urine test at home today and I’ll ring you back this afternoon for the result. When did you last have sex without a condom? … More than three weeks ago — good, then a negative test is reliable."

(At the call-back.) "Your test’s negative, and you’re taking it correctly — so I can reassure you for real: with desogestrel, about one in five women have periods that become infrequent or stop altogether, and others bleed irregularly. It’s expected, it’s harmless, and it does NOT mean the pill’s failing."

"Just so you’re covered: take it within the same 12-hour window daily. If you’re more than 12 hours late, take it and use condoms for two days. Being sick soon after a pill, or bad diarrhoea, can count like a missed pill — the leaflet gives the exact time limit."

"While you’re here — are you due your smear, any need for STI testing, and is this method working for you overall? If the bleeding pattern ever bothers you, there are other options like the implant or coil."
"So: not pregnant, periods stopping is normal on this. If you ever miss pills, get pregnancy symptoms, or just want peace of mind, do a test and come back. You did exactly the right thing checking."

f.learning: Absent or erratic periods on the desogestrel progestogen-only pill are common, acceptable and expected — about 1 in 5 users have infrequent or absent bleeding (desogestrel SPC) and others have more frequent or irregular bleeding, none of which is harmful or a sign the pill is failing — so accurate reassurance is appropriate, but only AFTER excluding pregnancy. The governing principle is "reassure, but test first": before reassuring, screen for missed or late pills (desogestrel has a 12-hour window), vomiting or diarrhoea around the time of a pill, interacting medications (enzyme inducers) and pregnancy symptoms, and arrange a pregnancy test wherever there is any doubt about adherence or any symptom (a home urine test reported back when the consultation is by video; reliable from 3 weeks after the last unprotected sex), because confident blind reassurance is the trap. Review correct use and reinforce the missed-pill rules (a pill more than 12 hours late is "missed" — take it, continue, and use condoms/abstain for 48 hours; vomiting soon after a pill (within the CoSRH POP time limit) or severe diarrhoea is treated as a possible missed pill; understand emergency contraception). Use the consultation for a wider sexual-health review (STI risk and testing, cervical screening status, and whether the method still suits her — considering LARC such as an implant or IUS if the bleeding pattern is bothersome), and address her actual concern, which is anxiety about an unknown pregnancy: once the test is negative and use correct, give clear, explained reassurance and state what would warrant rechecking. The hidden agenda is pregnancy anxiety, possibly with unspoken questions about method suitability or future fertility; take it seriously, resolve it with the test, and give informed reassurance plus a method review rather than waving it away.

knowledge.guideline: CoSRH Progestogen-only Pills guideline (August 2022, amended April 2026) · CoSRH Emergency Contraception guideline (2017, amended) · CoSRH Problematic Bleeding with Hormonal Contraception (2015)
knowledge.summary: Absent or infrequent bleeding is a common, harmless effect of desogestrel and not a sign the pill has failed — but amenorrhoea can also hide a pregnancy, so check adherence and test before reassuring.

points.t: Irregular, infrequent or absent bleeding is common on desogestrel and is not harmful. Absent periods do not mean the pill has stopped working. Explain this at the start of any POP and again when it happens.

CoSRH POP (2022): amenorrhoea may mask a pregnancy. Ask about late or missed pills, vomiting or severe diarrhoea, new medicines (especially enzyme inducers) and pregnancy symptoms. If there is any doubt, a urine pregnancy test — reliable from 3 weeks after the last unprotected sex.

CoSRH POP (2022): a desogestrel pill more than 12 hours late counts as missed — take it as soon as remembered, continue daily, and use condoms or avoid sex for 48 hours. Emergency contraception may be needed if she had sex after the missed pill before 48 hours of correct pill-taking.

Vomiting soon after a pill or severe diarrhoea may stop absorption — follow the CoSRH POP time limits and treat it as a possible missed pill. Enzyme-inducing drugs reduce effectiveness; check any new medicine against the BNF.
Offer STI testing according to risk and check that cervical screening is up to date. If the bleeding pattern bothers her, discuss other methods including the implant or intrauterine options.
A positive test needs same-week review of options and early pregnancy care. Pelvic pain with a positive test needs same-day assessment to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

model.text: Yes, that’s what I want.

model.text: Mostly in the morning. I think I’ve been good, but I can’t swear I’ve never been late.

model.text: Not that I remember, but I couldn’t be certain.
Any vomiting or bad diarrhoea in the last few months, or any new medicines — including herbal remedies like St John’s wort?
No, nothing like that.
And any signs that might suggest pregnancy — sickness, sore breasts, needing to wee more, feeling different?
Not really. I’m just anxious.
What’s behind the worry — what would a pregnancy mean for you right now?

model.text: It’s not the right time. I just want to know the pill’s actually working.
That makes complete sense. Let’s get you a definite answer rather than a guess.
model.why: Validates and commits to resolving the uncertainty

model.text: Because you can’t be completely sure about timing, I’d like you to do a urine pregnancy test today. They’re reliable from three weeks after sex without extra protection. Do you have one at home, or shall we arrange one here?
model.why: Tests first; explains reliability window; practical on video

model.text: I can get one from the chemist on the way home.

Perfect. Now, why periods stop: this pill thins the womb lining, so there’s often very little to shed. Bleeding changes are really common — some women bleed irregularly, some rarely, some not at all. None of that is harmful, and it doesn’t mean the pill has stopped working.

model.text: So no period doesn’t mean something’s wrong?

Exactly — once the test is negative, you can trust that. Just so you’re covered in future: if you’re ever more than 12 hours late, take the pill as soon as you remember, carry on as normal, and use condoms for the next two days. If you had sex in that time, get in touch because you might need emergency contraception. Being sick soon after a pill or bad diarrhoea can count as missing one too.
model.why: CoSRH missed-pill rules and emergency contraception

model.text: While we’re talking, can I check a couple of other things? Would an STI check be useful for you, and is your smear test up to date?
I’d need to check on the smear. An STI test wouldn’t hurt.

I’ll send you the link for a sexual-health test kit, and we can check your screening status on the record. And overall — does this pill suit you? If remembering it every day or the bleeding pattern ever bothers you, there are options like the implant or a coil that you don’t have to think about.
model.why: Method review and LARC offered, not imposed

model.text: I’m happy with it for now, I think. Maybe I’ll look at the implant.
That’s fine — I’ll send you some information and you can decide in your own time.
So — can you tell me what you’re going to do after this call?
Do a test today. If it’s negative, stop worrying — no periods is normal on this. If I’m more than 12 hours late, condoms for two days.

Exactly. If the test is positive, contact us straight away so we can talk through options — and if you ever have a positive test with tummy pain on one side or bleeding, that needs urgent same-day assessment. Otherwise, keep going as you are.
model.why: Safety-net for positive result and ectopic warning

model.text: Thanks. I feel much calmer.

social.t: A possible pregnancy carries different meaning for each woman. Ask, don’t assume, and be ready to discuss all options if the test is positive.

legal.t: Contraception and sexual-health consultations are confidential; GMC confidentiality guidance applies. Sexual-health clinic records are held separately.

professional.t: Reassurance must rest on evidence — here, a negative test and correct use. Document the missed-pill discussion and the advice given.
Use contraception reviews to check STI risk, cervical screening and method satisfaction.

community.t: Community pharmacy for pregnancy tests and emergency contraception; local sexual-health services and online STI testing; LARC fitting services.

What a pregnancy would mean to her now

playbook.diagnosis: Amenorrhoea on desogestrel — very likely an expected progestogenic effect, to be confirmed by excluding pregnancy.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This pill keeps the lining of the womb thin, so there’s often nothing to shed. That’s why periods can stop. It’s safe, and it doesn’t mean the pill isn’t working — once the test confirms you’re not pregnant.”

management.psychosocial: Resolve the anxiety with a test, give her the rules to feel in control, and review the method without pressure.
sharedPlan: Urine pregnancy test today (reliable from 3 weeks after unprotected sex)
If negative: continue desogestrel; reinforce the 12-hour, 48-hour and EC rules
STI testing by risk; check cervical screening; information on implant and intrauterine options
safetyNet: Positive test — contact the practice straight away

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you reassure safely. Candidates fail by reassuring without testing, by quoting the wrong pill rules, or by turning a simple worry into a lecture. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: “That’s just the pill” — no adherence questions and no test.
items.why: Amenorrhoea can mask pregnancy (CoSRH POP 2022). Blind reassurance is unsafe.
items.fix: Ask about late pills, vomiting, medicines and symptoms; arrange a pregnancy test.

items.fail: Giving the 3-hour window or forgetting the 48-hour rule.
items.why: Desogestrel has a 12-hour window; late pills need 48 hours of extra precautions.
items.fix: “More than 12 hours late: take it, carry on, condoms for two days.”

items.fail: Testing too early and reassuring on a negative result.
items.why: A urine test is reliable only from 3 weeks after the last unprotected sex.
items.fix: Explain the window and when to repeat the test if needed.

items.fail: Ignoring “I’m paranoid” and moving straight to pill rules.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” The anxiety is the reason she came.
items.fix: Ask what a pregnancy would mean to her, then commit to a definite answer.

items.fail: Turning the consultation into a lecture on every contraceptive method.
items.why: Poor time management and not tailored to her agenda.
items.fix: Offer the implant or coil briefly, send information, and let her decide.

items.fail: No plan for a positive result.
items.fix: “If it’s positive, contact us today — and pain or bleeding with a positive test needs same-day assessment.”

timeMap.d: She tells you she is paranoid about pregnancy. State the principle: test first, then reassure.
Routine, late or missed pills (12-hour window), vomiting or diarrhoea, new medicines, pregnancy symptoms.
What a pregnancy would mean now; she wants to trust the pill.
Urine test today, reliable from 3 weeks. Why periods stop on desogestrel. Missed-pill and EC rules.
STI check, screening status, method review with LARC offered, teach-back, positive-test and ectopic safety-net.

wordPics.fail: “That’s just the pill, don’t worry” with no questions and no test; wrong missed-pill window; no emergency contraception advice; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Asks about missed pills and symptoms, arranges a pregnancy test, explains that amenorrhoea is expected, and gives the 12-hour rule.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains why periods stop, the 3-week test window, the 48-hour and EC rules; checks interactions; offers STI testing and screening review; discusses LARC without pressure; teach-back; clear plan if the test is positive, including the ectopic warning.

avoid.dont: "That’s completely normal on the mini-pill — nothing to worry about."
avoid.instead: "It’s usually normal — let’s make sure with a test, then I can reassure you properly."
avoid.why: Blind reassurance is the trap in this station; it fails Tasks.

avoid.dont: "You have three hours to take it."
avoid.why: The 3-hour rule is for traditional POPs; wrong rules undermine safe use.

avoid.dont: "You should really switch to the implant."
avoid.instead: "If the bleeding or daily pill ever bothers you, the implant or a coil are options."
avoid.why: She is happy with her method; pushing LARC is not patient-centred.

community.t: Community pharmacy for pregnancy tests and emergency contraception; local sexual-health services and online STI testing; LARC fitting services.

redFlags: Any doubt about adherence, vomiting or interacting drugs — test before reassuring
Positive test with one-sided pelvic pain or bleeding — same-day assessment for ectopic pregnancy
Sex after a missed pill before 48 hours of correct use — consider emergency contraception
psychosocial: Pill routine and how she remembers it
What a pregnancy would mean to her now
ice: Idea: “No periods might be normal — or I might be pregnant.”
Expectation: to know whether this is normal

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Amenorrhoea on desogestrel — very likely an expected progestogenic effect, to be confirmed by excluding pregnancy.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “This pill keeps the lining of the womb thin, so there’s often nothing to shed. That’s why periods can stop. It’s safe, and it doesn’t mean the pill isn’t working — once the test confirms you’re not pregnant.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried you could be pregnant without knowing — so let’s find out for certain today, rather than me just telling you not to worry.”
management.psychosocial: Resolve the anxiety with a test, give her the rules to feel in control, and review the method without pressure.
sharedPlan: Urine pregnancy test today (reliable from 3 weeks after unprotected sex)
If negative: continue desogestrel; reinforce the 12-hour, 48-hour and EC rules
STI testing by risk; check cervical screening; information on implant and intrauterine options
safetyNet: Positive test — contact the practice straight away
Positive test with pain or bleeding — urgent same-day assessment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you reassure safely. Candidates fail by reassuring without testing, by quoting the wrong pill rules, or by turning a simple worry into a lecture. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: “That’s just the pill” — no adherence questions and no test.
items.why: Amenorrhoea can mask pregnancy (CoSRH POP 2022). Blind reassurance is unsafe.
items.fix: Ask about late pills, vomiting, medicines and symptoms; arrange a pregnancy test.

items.fail: Giving the 3-hour window or forgetting the 48-hour rule.
items.why: Desogestrel has a 12-hour window; late pills need 48 hours of extra precautions.
items.fix: “More than 12 hours late: take it, carry on, condoms for two days.”

items.fail: Testing too early and reassuring on a negative result.
items.why: A urine test is reliable only from 3 weeks after the last unprotected sex.
items.fix: Explain the window and when to repeat the test if needed.

items.fail: Ignoring “I’m paranoid” and moving straight to pill rules.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” The anxiety is the reason she came.
items.fix: Ask what a pregnancy would mean to her, then commit to a definite answer.

items.fail: Turning the consultation into a lecture on every contraceptive method.
items.why: Poor time management and not tailored to her agenda.
items.fix: Offer the implant or coil briefly, send information, and let her decide.

items.fail: No plan for a positive result.
items.fix: “If it’s positive, contact us today — and pain or bleeding with a positive test needs same-day assessment.”
